utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before I give the floor to Defence counsel, who will conduct their examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we will be following here. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel for Brigadier Kubura. We have been told by the Defence that they will need 40 or 45 minutes for their examination-in-chief. Once they have completed their examination-in-chief I will give the floor to the Prosecution, who are to your right. The Prosecutor will also put questions to you, probably for the same length of time. Once the Prosecution has completed its cross-examination, Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura may re-examine you. There is another Defence team defending General Hadzihasanovic, who may also ask you questions. Once all these questions have been put to you the Judges, who are sitting before you, may, if they deem it necessary and if they believe it's in the interest of justice, put questions to you, the purpose of which is to clarify answers that you have given or to fill in gaps that we feel that your testimony contains. I would also like to mention two other important factors. You have taken the solemn declaration and you have said that you will speak the truth, which means that you should not give false testimony. False testimony is a punishable offence. In addition, there is another provision that I should mention; it's a complicated provision but I will try to explain it to you in the clearest possible terms. When a question is put to you, if you feel that your answer could be subsequently used against you to incriminate you, you can say that you don't want to answer the question. You may refuse to answer the question. However, in such a case, and we have never had such cases to date, but I must mention this possibility because it's always something that could happen, in this case the Trial Chamber may compel you to answer the question; however, you are granted a form of immunity. Whatever you say can't be used against you. As the procedure that we follow here is an oral procedure based on your testimony, Defence may show you documents, military documents for example, and ask you to identify the documents and comment on them. If you feel that a question is too complicated or if you fail to understand a question, ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase it. If you encounter any difficulties in the course of your testimony, don't hesitate to mention the fact. For technical reasons we have to have a break every hour and a half. As we started the hearing at 11.10 -- or as we resumed at 10 past 11.00, we will have a break at about half past 12.00. So there will only be one break today. If everything goes smoothly, if the schedule is respected by all the parties, it might not be necessary for you to return tomorrow if we complete your examination today; if not, you will have to return tomorrow. Without wasting anymore time, I will now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Adilovic, I would like to ask you to speak up when you answer the questions, and to make a brief pause after I put a question to you. This should make it easier for the interpreters to do their job. In response to a question to the Presiding Judge you said where you were in 1992 and 1993, so I will very briefly repeat the question. In 1992, from the time that the war broke out, where were you in fact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Vitez, and in 1992 I immediately joined the Territorial Defence Staff in Vitez. A volunteer detachment was established and I joined that detachment. I remained in the Vitez Territorial Defence Staff and I went into the field of Visoko. I remained there until I was transferred to the 7th Muslim Brigade. But I forwarded a written request to be transferred to the 7th Muslim Brigade, and that was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When did that take place and who granted you that request?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in November. That took place in November. I don't know the name of the officials who granted me leave, but when I was granted this leave I think that Haso Ribo was the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I became a member of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were you assigned to any particular company?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Since at the very beginning the units weren't up to strength and when I left Vitez I was -- I had been a platoon commander down there, so in the 7th Muslim Brigade -- in the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade I thought that I would be a platoon commander or a company commander. And this is what I had been led to believe. Since the unit wasn't up to strength, they waited for a certain period of time for the unit to be brought up to strength and for me to be appointed as a company commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as a platoon commander or as a company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you deployed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I was staying in my house, and when I reported to the 1st Battalion, I would go to the barracks. I would report there. That was a temporary situation, and then I would go home on leave and so on and so forth until I was permanently assigned to a unit or rather a company. After I had been assigned to a company, I was issued tasks, and I had to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your battalion, or rather company, did it have any particular zone of responsibility in Travnik or in the greater Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Our unit did have a zone of responsibility; it was above Travnik in the village called Bijelo Bucje and that was the zone we had. It faced the Serbs who were up there and the men were rotated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave we would like to show the witness the map so that he can indicate the exact location of his company during this period of time. This is the only document that we will be using in the course of our examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Adilovic, could you please have a look at the map and mark the exact location of the Bijelo Bucje. Mark the location with a felt-tipped. You can use the pen to mark the location with a circle.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: How far was this area from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how far it was exactly, perhaps about 15 kilometres or so. But there were other roads leading from Travnik to Bijelo Bucje, other roads which had to be used for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just mark this location with a number 1 above the location.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Above.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Adilovic, in the course of your proofing we discussed document P11, instructions to the Muslim fighter. And I asked you then and I'm asking you now whether you've ever seen this booklet before.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I only saw that booklet during preparations, but at that time I never saw it nor did a single member of my unit see that booklet or anyone else. If anyone had seen such booklet, I would probably have known of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you said in the course of the preparations, you mean in the course of the preparations for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Adilovic, are you a religious man?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of April or in mid-April 1993, where were you and what establishment post did you have, Mr. Adilovic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of April or in mid-April 1993, where were you together with your unit and what establishment post did you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was a company commander; that was my establishment post. I was the commander of a company that was from Vitez since I am from Vitez. So the entire company was from Vitez. And about the 10th of April I was assigned a task, or rather I was on temporary leave -- at the time I was on leave and my task was to go to the Bijelo Bucje area of responsibility to replace a unit of ours, or rather a company of ours. I arrived in Travnik with the unit on the 10th of April. And naturally we went to the barracks to prepare so that I could prepare to go into the field. That's where we were issued with weapons and that's where we prepared and we waited for the right time to leave the barracks and go to Bijelo Bucje. Since at the time there was tension because of the HVO and for security reasons, it was decided that I should remain in the barracks until we could examine the situation as far as the HVO was concerned, until the situation calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In mid-April something happened that affected the situation in Travnik in a particular manner. Isn't that correct? I'm referring to your company and to your troops.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In mid-April, was there an event of some kind that in some way disturbed your men or affected the morale of the men in your unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said I was there on the 10th, but on the 16th I was in the barracks. I was in the barracks up until the 16th of April. And since the attack had already been carried out on Ahmici, on the village of Ahmici, my men in the unit were upset since 99 per cent of the soldiers were from Vitez and they didn't want to go to Bijelo Bucje. They had requested to be allowed to return home to see what the situation was as far as their families were concerned. My family was also in Vitez. And on that very same day I found out that my wife had been wounded and I also asked to return to Vitez. Since the main roads had been blocked and it wasn't possible to travel from Travnik to Vitez by using those roads, I asked -- I wanted to travel over -- to go via the hills, to reach the village of Poculica which is where we would collect soldiers when I had to go into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were you authorised by the battalion command to go there with your unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had to ask for their authorisation, because as I have said weapons had been left in the barracks and the men weren't allowed to go home without their weapons and the weapons had to be left there [as interpreted]; that was the order. But I then had to ask the battalion commander to allow us to have weapons and ammunition. I didn't know which route I would take. I didn't what would happen to me. I didn't know whether anyone would be waiting for me. And thank God I was authorised to do what I wanted to do. I managed to reach Poculica with the unit without having to engage in combat of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Given the passage of time, can you now remember how long after the events in Ahmici you set off with your unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three days after that event. I can't be precise, but it was two or three days later while waiting for the procedural matters to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you inform the Chamber and tell us where Poculica is located?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You can use the map to indicate the location. You can use a felt-tipped to encircle the location.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it with number 2.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: How many men did you set off from Travnik with and how many men did you reach Poculica with? What was the strength of your unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: There were about a hundred men in my company, but not everyone went into the field. About 70 of them set off. Ten men remained at home. I set off from Travnik with that unit. We set off in the direction of Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached there did you establish contact with any other ABiH unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Which unit was that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: When I reached Poculica I established contact with the 325th Brigade and I informed the brigade command, or rather at that time I spoke to Halil Brzina, person in my unit was re-subordinated to the 325th Brigade and I was given responsibility in the zone of Sljivcica. In the zone of responsibility I carried out rotations for the 325th. Of the hundred men I had, I formed a shift for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had the zone of responsibility and that you were subordinated to 325th Brigade. Where is Sljivcica located? Could you point to its location on the map. If there is a larger place there, could you mark it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't find it, but it's above Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is Sivrino Selo, Sivrino village on the map?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it then, please.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the location with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that period of time how far away was the zone of responsibility encompassing Sivrino Selo and Sljivcica from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about 20 kilometres from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that you informed the brigade commander Mr. Halil Brzina. What sort of duties did Halil Brzina have at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what his duties were. I'm not sure but I know that I turned to him on a number of occasions, I contacted him on a number of occasions. I felt close to him, but I couldn't really tell you exactly what his duties were. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: How long did your company remain in that field, during which period of time was it there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: My company remained in that area of responsibility right up until July, I think. I couldn't tell you what the exact month was, but I remained there until the road between the brigade command and the 1st Battalion command became passable. When this road was opened up, I then immediately joined the battalion and participated in other activities within the framework of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was after the events in June 1993 in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you arrived in that area a few days after the events in Ahmici. Could you be more precise. What was the date, what was the period of time if events took place in Ahmici on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: The events in Ahmici took place on the 16th, and it's around that time that I set off. It was around the 18th. I arrived on the 20th or around the 20th in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Was that in April?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Between the 20th of April, 1993, after the events in Travnik, a tumultuous month in 1993. After that month were you engaged in any kind of combat in that area?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't engaged in combat activity of any kind, apart from that I had to control the area of responsibility. But as my family was down below, my wife had been wounded, I took upon myself certain responsibilities, I made sure that shifts functions in the area of responsibility, and I made efforts to get my family members and the Bosniak people out of my settlement. So I worked on that for about 20 days until I managed to get my wife, children, and some people from my settlement out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As the company commander did you have a report from that period of time that, from the 20th of April until the end of June, and that's the amount of time you spent in that area, did you have any information, any reports, that there was combat in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you went back to Travnik when communication was set up between Travnik and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out afterwards when you got back to Travnik where the rest of the battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was engaged?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I found out from fighters that they participated in action at Hajdareve Njive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Ramo Durmis?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know him yourself?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but since it is a man - how should I put this? - an irresponsible man, I was not very close friends with him. But I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he left the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: He left the 7th Muslim Brigade, according to my memory it was in January. I never saw him again afterwards, nor did I have an opportunity to sit down and talk to him or anything like that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And so it was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President. And I would just like to ask the witness to sign the map and indicate the date as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Defence wish to tender this map into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Do the other Defence team members have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. Registrar, a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is Defence document for Mr. Kubura, D436 [as interpreted]. [In English] It will be my pleasure to announce this into English. This exhibit is admitted into the evidence under the reference DK36. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the other lawyers like to ask any questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the time being, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am turning to the Prosecution now -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise to my learned friend. There is a mistake in the transcript. It is DK36, not DK436.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Adilovic. I just have a few questions to you; it shouldn't take that long. I'm not entirely clear about the date you became a company commander. It must have been sometime in November, perhaps sometime later. Can you specify when it was that you became a company commander? I'm not talking about the Territorial Defence of Vitez; I'm talking about the 7th Muslim -- Mountain Muslim Brigade, that is.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was by the end of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it was within the 1st Battalion of the 7th Mountain Muslim Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many companies there were with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could answer the question again I had asked before because the interpreters didn't pick it up. My question was whether that -- you know, the company was within the 1st Battalion of the 7th Mountain Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how many -- how many companies does the 1st Battalion have at the time you were one of the company commanders?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: There were four companies, but they were not up to full strength in terms of their establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe you told us your company had hundred soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the other companies, did they have more or less than hundred soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: A lot less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the strength in numbers. How much less?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: The other companies numbered between 50 and 60 men, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your company which you were leading from February 1993 onwards, did it have a name, a number? Was it the 1st Company, the 2nd?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: It was called the Vitez Company and it was the 4th Company as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The other companies, did they also have names according to where the people came from like the Vitez Company in your case? How were the other companies called, if they had names?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: They were called by their name -- numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 1st one, 2nd one, 3rd, one, and then the 4th one being the Vitez Company?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your company did you have platoons or detachments?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Within the company I had detachments and departments -- platoons rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many detachments were there within your company?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: It would be easier for me to say how many platoons were within detachments. We had three detachments and three platoons per each detachment. The 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, for the 1st one, and then for the 2nd one, 1, 2, 3 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who was your battalion commander at the time you were the command of the 4th Vitez Company?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment it was Fadil Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was he the battalion commander throughout the time you were the company commander or did he change?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Not the whole time. There were changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was followed by Safet Junozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there a time that Safit Terzic [as interpreted] was also a commander of the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us that on 10th of April you were supposed to replace a unit at Bijelo Bucje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember which unit you were supposed to replace?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the company commander Suad --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the name, unfortunately, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the full name. The interpreters couldn't catch you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember the first name of the commander -- well, it was Jusovic, Suad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just to clear something up, you said that after the events in Ahmici you and your unit, you know, were transferred to another area and you have circled that area, and it was around Poculica and you also indicated that you were also at Sivrino Selo. And you told us that the time frame was from front of April, when you arrived, until I believe sometime in July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: So I said when I got to Poculica it's a location where -- when I was supposed to go out to the field I used to gather my men. And my area of responsibility was in Sljivcica and Sivrino Selo, and I had that territory under control. I can't remember the date, but I stayed there for as long as -- we had no communication between the brigade command and the battalion command, between Zenica and Travnik that is. When that communication was established, I went back to the battalion command, that is to say the units within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you say there was no communication between the brigade and the battalion command, you, your unit, had contacts with the battalion command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: My unit had contact with the brigade command but not with the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, where was the battalion command located at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the mission your company was given, you as the commander, in that area? What were you supposed to do there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: My task was simply to stop the advance of the HVO forces in the direction of Poculica village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was Poculica village so important that it needed to be defended? Why would the HVO advance to that village?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why, but it was important to defend Poculica, it was important to me. And I stayed there to defend Poculica. When I got there I didn't go to there to go to sleep. I participated in the activities of the 325th. In order to have this area of responsibility under control, in order to stop the HVO from advancing, but why that area was interesting to them I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were hundred soldiers in that village or in the wider area, more or less?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many civilians were living in that area, the area you had under control at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know Poculica is a village. There is Prnjavor and Vrhovine. I can't tell you exactly how many. But those soldiers were my soldiers from these areas, Poculica, Lupac, and so on and so forth. So it was easier. I mean, some of them could go home and sow the crops, et cetera, and I had another shift from another village and they could stay at home. There were no combat activities in terms of advancing or pushing back the HVO forces. There was nothing like that at the time. We were simply trying to stop them from making any advances themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember how many women and children there were in that village?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was the normal population living there, and the way it had always been. There were women and children and everybody else. Apart from that there were some refugees from Vitez who came up there and they were housed there, so I can't tell you exactly how many houses or how many families or how many refugees or anything else. But it was densely populated and there were quite a few people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the men, the local men, were part of your company, the men of fighting age?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Those who were fit to fight, I mean not all of them. Some of them were in the 325th. So a part of that population, a hundred people from the villages, Lupac, Preocica, Vrhovine, Poculica, and so on. So from that detachment area, about a hundred people who made up my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So people who were fighting age were either deployed in your company or in another part of the -- or the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just to be entirely sure, you told us that you were part of the 325th Brigade. You were resubordinated or deployed as part of the 325th Brigade, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that I was a member of the 325th; I was a member of the Territorial Defence Staff Vitez. On the occasion of the setting up of brigades and corps at that stage, I joined the 7th Muslim Brigade. However, since I got there to that area, my area of responsibility, the one that was assigned to me, was within the area of responsibility of the 325th and they gave me a part of that area in which to stop the advance of the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were -- you talked to Mr. Halil Brzina. I think you said he was a person you trusted over that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I said I talked to him. I told him I got there and about the situation of my family and all that. I explained all that to him and I asked for the Red Cross to -- for Red Cross assistance through him in order for my family to be saved because I knew that my wife had been wounded and -- in Vitez, and that there were other people who were wounded. So I asked him for assistance to help me, to somehow reach my family and get them out of that inferno and to remain within the area of responsibility of the 325th and to stay here in that area of responsibility, that area Sljivcica and Sivrino Selo are close to my home, so I could follow the events there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While you were there, did you have contacts with Mr. Brzina, or was it just in the beginning while you were sent there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Only in the beginning. Only in the beginning. Basically I talked to him and then he wrote to the Red Cross. And then I was assigned my area of responsibility and I stuck to it, and I concentrated on the well-being of my family and the Bosniak people who were our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. Halil Brzina, he was the deputy brigade commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that nor do I remember that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, there is some information that he may have been the assistant commander for logistics in that time period. So that's not something which you were aware of at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I was with the battalion command and according to the brigade command, and I mean what it was all about, I was not really interested in all that. I didn't need to know who was there. It was a higher level. I didn't care about that. I cared about my own responsibility, which was at the battalion; that was my job. And I got my tasks assigned from the battalion, and so I was responsible for my own unit and I was responsible and accountable to the battalion commander and no one else and it was up to him and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go back, or rather forward to Mr. Ramo Durmis. You have been asked about him and I believe you said sort of you lost contact in January 1993. Now, were you involved in an action on the 28th December, 1992, in the area of Visoko and Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, at Visoko. But not at that time. I was not -- I mean, at that time I was not a company commander. I just went up there with the commanders and I followed the activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to be clear, on the 28th of December, 1992, when there was some type of action in the Visoko area, you were a part of that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because we do have a report by Mr. Ramo Durmis in which he mentions you as being present there. So that would -- that would be correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I've never seen such a report until the proofing, and what I did see -- I mean as to whether I was there, well it is correct that I was there. And as to everything else, I really don't believe any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When is it the last time that you have seen Mr. Ramo Durmis?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I said at some point in January straight afterwards, straight after Visoko on the 28th of December. That was the last time I saw him and I never met him or had anything to do with him whatsoever, and I didn't even know where he was and what he was up to. But I did hear that he was no longer with the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And from whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: From soldiers, fighters, my own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why would they tell you something about Ramo Durmis? Was he a person of interest, prominence?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I myself actually argued with Ramo Durmis from the very start, when we first met; it was between the two of us. And I never, ever wanted to sit down, have a coffee, or talk to him, let alone participate in any sort of activity at his side, never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Never again after what time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: After the 28th of December when we got back from Visoko. It was in the month of January. We parted ways and I went to one side and I don't know what he did, where he took himself to. And afterwards I heard, as I said, that he was no longer with the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, we just heard from the previous witness that the operation in Visoko was successful and the units involved -- Mr. Ramo Durmis's unit was even commended for that action. The person who said that was the operations officer of the 7th Mountain Muslim Brigade. Do you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I disagree that it was all that successful; I think it was a failure in fact. And I don't know whether he got any awards or not. I never cared about it, especially anything having to do with Ramo Durmis. But from my personal point of view, it was not a success. It was a failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you ever in contacts with any foreign fighters where Arab countries or from Turkish countries? In your capacity as a company commander, were you in contacts?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpretation. Well, I've never had any contacts, either myself or my unit, and I believe that no one from our battalion had any contacts with any foreigners, or foreign members as we called them. I myself can guarantee that I myself or members of my unit or the battalion have never had anything to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How is it possible you can speak for the battalion? You can certainly talk about your company, but how can you talk about the other three companies? What makes you so certain that, number 1, number 2, number 3 didn't have contact with these fighters?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we changed shifts and spent time at the barracks, the 1st and the 2nd Company, I mean, I got to know these people. And on that basis I can make this claim, and I've never seen anyone coming to the battalion command in the company of any such people; that's the basis of my claim. Okay, it is true that I am at the company level and I am accountable for what the company does, but I do know of about things taking place around me and I know this has never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you aware that one of the staff officers of the brigade said in August that people from the brigade -- battalion got used to the foreign fighters and that they in fact liked their presence because it makes them more secure? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've never heard anything like that. I've never heard of any staff officer having been quoted as saying that, and my learned colleague has not told the witness who is supposed to have said that and when. So I don't know what it's all about. This may confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is P610. It's a document from the assistant commander for morale, Mr. Ahmet Adilovic, and I can show it to the witness and perhaps that can -- he can have a comment and say, yes, I change my opinion, or no I haven't heard about that. It can be shown to the witness, I have no problem; P610 please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please give us P610.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, we do have an additional copy -- in fact, for everybody in the courtroom if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Mr. Ahmet Adilovic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember what his position was at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think he was responsible for the morale of the soldiers but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And if you look at the first part of the document you see it's a document entitled "Report on BM," apparently, "combat morale situation." And it's sent to the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. It dates 4th August, 1993. And let me -- I'm just interested in paragraph 4, if you can go down to paragraph 4. And here it says what I asked you before and I can read it slowly to you: "In addition to these, the following are specific factors for the 1st Battalion, 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade," and that's your battalion, Mr. Adilovic. Then A: "To date they have got used to the Arabs and also some Turks taking part in B/D with them. Their presence makes them more secure and the Arabs were frequently of decisive importance for the success of an action. So the soldiers of the 1st Battalion, 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade wanted them engaged again in B/D with members of the 1st Battalion, 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade." My question to you is just: Does that also apply to your unit, that you, you know, felt more secure when these people were present? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Within my unit, and I've said this before, there were no foreign participants of any sort. So I can't tell you how my unit felt without or with them since we were never with them, they [Realtime transcript read in error "we"] were never there in my unit. So these were only and exclusively the people from the area that I've just described. And as to this report, I mean it's up to him, up to the author of that report. I don't know to whom he had talked. He never contacted my unit for the purposes of this report. I mean, that's from the brigade commander; it is his opinion. Perhaps a couple of people did think like that. I am able to argue about this, but I am unaware of this. And I do know that there were no foreign members or foreigners within my unit; I can claim that and I stand by it. And as to what people may have wished for or not wished for, that's altogether a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only reason I show you the document is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't want to interrupt my colleague, but there's an error in the transcript, page 69, line 17 the witness said "they were never in my unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only point is, Mr. Adilovic, I don't dispute what you said about your company; I was just wary about the fact that you wanted to speak on behalf of the whole battalion. And this document seems to contradict what you said about the rest of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you now. I don't know. I was never familiar with the way that this document was drafted. I don't know whether there were discussions of any kind. There were no discussions with my unit. I don't know on the basis of what this report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to have a break now. Does Defence counsel have any additional questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our break now and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura have said that they have no additional questions for the witness. I will now turn to General Hadzihasanovic's Defence counsel. Do you have any additional questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I have a few brief questions I would like to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me when you retired what was the rank that you held?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't even say that I retired. I left the Federation army in 2001 in the month of September. I'm unemployed. I'm not retired. I left with the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you left the army in 2001 of your own accord. Could you tell me what the first name of your father was.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: His first name is Sefik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well because there is a document with two individuals with the same first name. I will show you P498, which is a list of the members of the 7th Brigade. This document, which is a list of members of the 7th Brigade, could you have a look at page 3, please, and your name is on page 3 of that document. It says that the 1st Battalion, the 1st Company, the 1st Detachment on the 28th of October there's Ramo Durmis, the 1st Company, the 1st -- on the 1st of February 1993 is Suad Jusovic. The 3rd Company, 1st Detachment, 15th of January, 1993, Rezad Skopljak; and then the 1st Company, commander of the 2nd Detachment, the 10th of January, 1993, Asim Bektas. And you appear as the commander of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Detachment, the 10th of December, 1992. Were you appointed on the 5th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I didn't have these duties. As I have said, these were assumptions on the strength of the units. But towards the end of February at the beginning of March, I took over this company from Bektas, Asim, and this isn't the name of my father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English translation that I have of the first name of your father it says Sekib. Was there a mistake made?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: My father's name was Sefik, not Sekib.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sefik, because you say that the 5th of December, 1992, is not the right date. You assumed command in February, not before. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question put to you a minute ago you said that there were four companies. When one has a look at this document, I can see that there is a 1st Company, a 2nd Company, and a 3rd Company. Where's the 4th Company?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. This isn't clear to me here below. It says the 1st Company then the 2nd Company. This part isn't clear. According to this document, there were two other companies. You can see it says "the commander of the 2nd Company Suad Jusovic." The commander of the other company was Adlo, Enver, son of Sekib.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When reading this document it would appear, as you say, that there are -- that in the 2nd Company there is one detachment with Suad Jusovic at its head, and in the other detachment you seem to be at its head. Can you explain that, since Suad Jusovic can be seen above as the deputy commander since he is referred to as the deputy. And there's the date, the 13th of December, 1993. Would Fadil Hadic be the deputy, and Naim Horo, Osman Osmanovic, Suad Jusovic, these individuals would be the deputies. In your opinion this document is not quite correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: It's not at all correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name -- but you say that this document doesn't reflect the actual situation. If I have understood you correctly, you were officially the commander of the 2nd Company as of the month of February, 1993, and not before that date?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Not of the second one. Asim Bektas was at the head of the Vitez 4th Company, which was called the 4th one. It was called the Vitez Company; that's the company that I took over at the end of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of February 1993. So you took charge of Bektas's company, the so-called Vitez Company. We take note of what you have just said. I'll move on to another subject now. In response to a question put to you, you said that the company was composed of about 100 men, roughly speaking. You were in charge of about a hundred men. While you performed your duties as commander and you started performing those duties at the end of February 1993, while performing those duties did your company sustain any losses in combat? Were there any men under you who were either killed or wounded in combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I assumed my duties we weren't involved in fighting. We held the area of responsibility and there were shifts. The area of responsibility was near Travnik in the village of Bijelo Bucje. So we weren't really involved in combat activities. And at that time I didn't have any men who had been wounded or killed. From March onwards, in March and April, in Sljivcica, some men were wounded by the HVO. There were -- there would be an exchange of fire, they would open fire from their lines. So there were a few such cases. A few men who were slightly wounded. They weren't seriously wounded. So during that period of time, I didn't sustain any losses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were on the slopes of Travnik in the area of responsibility, were you in the field around the clock or would you be present during the day and would you then return to sleep in your homes in the evening and then go back into the field into your zone of responsibility in the morning? How did this take place? Were you in the field on a permanent basis or did you come and go?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I took over the zone of responsibility with my unit in Bijelo Bucje. So I was on the front lines, but occasionally the men would have leave in the evening or they would rest near the line in dugouts, et cetera. Occasionally they would descend to the area where there are houses so that they could rest and so that I could have a rest, too. We would rest in those houses. We would have a shift and one shift would hold the line and another shift would be resting near the line, and then there were some men down below in those houses where they could also have a rest. That's How the men rotated in Bijelo Bucje. That's how we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you took up your position in Bijelo Bucje, was there a written order stating that your company was to take charge of that area? Was there a written order that you received or were you informed of the fact orally?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Bijelo Bucje as the army already had men involved in defence at the time, I can't say how this happened, but our battalion was assigned a zone of responsibility up there and, naturally, I arrived there with my unit. Our company was already holding the defence line up there and I only replaced that company. The men were rotated that company and then went to the battalion in Travnik and I would remain up there where I was in charge of that area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were on those slopes, what means of communication did you have with your headquarters? Did you have any radio sets? How did you inform your superior in the headquarters and his deputies of what was happening in the field? Or did you have communication problems?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: In Bijelo Bucje there was an advance detachment that monitored everything via the communications. Those were the communications with the battalion that we had. And up in the area of responsibility itself I did have problems because we didn't really have Motorolas. We didn't have much equipment to use as means of communication. Whenever it was necessary to contact the battalion command, I had to descend down below and inform the communications officer of the information that I had to relay. And I had to do this in order to receive a response. Occasionally sometimes I would say -- sometimes I had a Motorola, but this was quite rare. Sometimes I had a Motorola on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 7th Brigade, did the Chief of Staff assemble his company commanders for working meetings, for briefings? Did you assemble or did you never see each other?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I had working meetings with the battalion command alone. And later, in August 1993, I had a briefing with Mr. Amir Kubura. We were scattered all over the place, so it was a matter of becoming familiar with a unit commander's company commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the battalion commander, did he visit you in the field, see the sort of things you were involved in, to see what sort of difficulties you might encounter? Did your battalion commander visit you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He would come to visit the unit to have a look around and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the military police of the 7th Brigade, did you usually -- did you have any contact with them from time to time or did you never see them?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for me to have contact with them. I didn't meet them nor was I involved in any activities with them. It wasn't necessary for them to bring anyone in, et cetera. So as far as security was concerned, I didn't have any problems and I did not have to have much contact with them. I didn't have to have contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you had had a problem, who would you have informed of the fact within the 7th Brigade's military police unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: You would report to the command battalion. If a soldier had left the line, had failed to respond to a summons, I -- left my unit. And if I didn't know where he had gone, there's a certain procedure to be followed. If you want to go into another unit you need authorisation from another unit. But I have already said that I didn't have such problems so that I personally had to send reports to the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: When you were appointed or selected to become company commander, did you know for what reason you yourself had been selected, or did you yourself come forward?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I myself had come forward and asked to be commander. It was my own request, my personal request. I came along and I said, Okay, this is where I come from and I was a detachment commander and I wanted to have that post, company or a detachment commander. I asked for it, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you for your replies to my questions. Now I'd like to turn to the Prosecution. Would you like to ask any questions following the Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there's a couple.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 of that document, it lists the commander of the 1st Company, 1st detachment, and 2nd Company commander 1st Detachment, and so on. Now, let me ask you, is it possible that the battalion was divided into two detachments and then for each detachment there were several companies? That means for the 1st Detachment of the Battalion there was the 1st Company, the 2nd, and the 3rd one; and for the 2nd Detachment of the Battalion there was the 1st Company and the 2nd Company. And you were the commander of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Detachment of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And within your company, you then had, again, detachments. Is that a possible explanation of the way the situation was?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll reply to this question once again. If you have a battalion within a battalion, you can't have detachments. I've already mentioned on a number of occasions that before the fact -- because of the fact that we were not up to strength -- I mean, these are -- this is the situation from before. We were trying to have detachments first because a detachment is smaller than a battalion. And then we thought we would have two detachments and then a battalion. And this is the structure. This was probably the original idea, but it did not happen that way in practice. We had to have a brigade but you can't have battalions made of detachments. They could only be made up of companies. So this did not actually exist as such. Maybe this was the initial conception, these were the plans when the 7th Muslim Brigade or the 1st Battalion were first being planned and set up. So I really am not aware of this because for a certain period of time I was asking for more people to join in, et cetera, in order to be posted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just on this, if you look at the names listed as company commanders, Mr. Durmis, Jusovic, Skopljak and you, Mr. Adilovic, I understand, you came in later. These were company commanders at the time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: In the field -- no, it wasn't like that. You can have any papers you like, but I was not a company commander at the time. I became a company commander on the basis of a written order at the end of February when I took over from Asim Bektas, and I took over the Vitez Company, and at that stage I acted as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What did Asim Bektas do after you replaced him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: He went into logistics, something like that, I don't know, because he did not wish to continue as a company commander anymore. And since I am from that area, from Vitez, I was ordered to -- by the battalion command to organise the practicalities a bit better, going out into the field, going home, coming back, et cetera, and so to replace Asim Bektas, and Asim Bektas, well, I don't know what was with him, something in logistics, but what exactly he did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while you were there as the company commander after February 1993, Mr. Suad Jusovic was also company commander of a different company within the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: He was commander of that company, and I did say that on the 10th of April I was supposed to replace that company from the Bijelo Bucje position from Poculica. And I went in the direction of Travnik barracks and we waited a little bit, although I didn't go up there to replace him in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me finish. Before you were appointed the commander of this company in February, you said that in November you had filed a written request to join the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade to Mr. Haso Ribo and then you were, in fact -- became a member of that brigade. In what capacity were you a member of the brigade between November and February? What were you doing? What sub-unit of the brigade were you attached to before you became the commander of the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Right. I was not carrying out any duties on the basis of any documents, orders, or anything like that. I was within the unit within the battalion. I was following the situation of the units; that was my task until the setting up order -- gathering of the people from that battalion to former companies. So I followed the situation within the unit. I went to Bijelo Bucje, et cetera. And I said I went to Visoko. And I was simply following that action, nothing else, as a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which unit did you follow to Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Jusovic's or somebody else's -- I don't know who it was. Whenever a commander tells you, okay, go and take a look, check things out, whether there's a need for something, just check out the general state of the unit at Bijelo Bucje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were given a supervisory task in some sort? You were given the task to go there and see what's happening with this unit?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Those were orders given to us orally to check it out. I was not given any orders in writing, but I did carry out the tasks I was told to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who gave you the order to check things out in Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time Fadil Hadzic for the most part. I don't know who else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Fadil Hadzic, if you look at again page 3, you see him as the first deputy commander of the 1st Battalion. Would that be the Fadil Hadzic, son of Refik, who gave you the oral order to go to Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's him. But I don't know that he had this establishment post. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But he was --

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't even know that all those detachments existed as such. Within this whole effort of setting up a brigade and a battalion, I don't know that there were any detachments. I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but he was obviously in a position of authority to give you an order and you accepted it, Mr. Fadil Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He couldn't just tell me what to do in any old way. I mean, of course he was told certain things and then he issued his directions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the units you went to visit in Bijelo Bucje were units part of the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one clarification, and I'd like for the witness to be shown this document that he was looking at earlier. On it is DK36 for the Defence of Mr. Kubura. I have a copy here so he can take a look -- no, DK29. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Adilovic, you said that your company was called Vitez Company. If you take a look at the indication Bektas, Asim, Poculica, Vitez, was that the company that you inherited and that you took over?

utterances.speaker: ENVER ADILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. That's the one I took over from Asim.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. Your testimony is completed now. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague to answer the questions asked by the lawyers acting on behalf of General Kubura. You have also answered the questions from the Prosecution and my own questions as well. Now, on the Judges' behalf I would like to wish you a pleasant journey back home. So I would like to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. Now on tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, we still have two witnesses. We've managed to make up for the delay. Now I'd like to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have planned witness number 10 for tomorrow, number 10 on the list. We have indicated that the hearing should take about an hour and a half, and we will try and make sure that it's less than that. And for Thursday we've got witness number 12. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. So as I've already mentioned this morning, tomorrow morning we'll start with an ex parte hearing, which will last between 9.00 and 9.10. Then we'll have a technical break and then it will be my pleasure to see the Prosecution and Mr. Kubura's Defence team at quarter to 10.00. General Hadzihasanovic will be there at 9.00 and General Kubura will be joining us at quarter to 10.00. We still have a couple of minutes left. Would you like to deal with anything else at the moment? Nothing? So in that case, thank you all, and I'll see you back here at 9.00 tomorrow morning. And this is VP418 that I am giving back to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
